source_read: PMC HTML full text, PMC5945349 (author manuscript of Clin Psychol Rev 2018), body read in full in my own browser tab (abstract, untitled introduction, all sections, Discussion, Highlights, Acknowledgments, Contributors and Conflict of Interest notes); the paper has no tables or figures; reference entries looked up for the studies the claims rely on (Khan 2013 x2, Greenfield 2010, Greenfield 2014, Compton 2007, Korte 2011, Bornstein 2015, Agabio 2016, Becker 2017, Alvanzo 2014, Blanco 2013, Lewis 2014 x2, Haas 2000, Diehl 2007, Stoltman 2015, Edlund 2012, Smith 2015/2017, McHugh 2013, Randall 1999)

claims.overstatement: The 'difference from population surveys by who reaches treatment' is an earlier review's explanation (Becker, McClellan & Reed, 2017), which McHugh et al. adopt and put in terms of severity: women already in treatment probably have more severe disorders, and a subset of women may progress fast to severe disorders. The claim should attribute it. 'Mostly in treatment samples' is the review's own description, but the citation it gives for cannabis (Khan, Okuda, et al., 2013) is, by its reference title, a NESARC general-population analysis of alcohol dependence. So either the citation is a slip for the NESARC cannabis paper, or a general-population analysis is counted as a replication. Either way it sits uneasily with the review's statement that population surveys did not replicate telescoping.
claims.note: Substances confirmed: alcohol (Diehl 2007; Randall 1999), marijuana (Khan 2013; Lewis, Hoffman & Nixon 2014), cocaine (Haas & Peters 2000, drug-involved offenders) and prescription opioids (Lewis 2014); not heroin (Lewis 2014; Stoltman 2015, people not in treatment). Keyes 2010 is named as the population-based analysis that did not replicate. The review also states that women start use later (Keyes 2010; Greenfield 2010). It is a critical narrative review (search terms reused from Greenfield et al. 2007, 517 papers screened, no appraisal), and none of its telescoping studies are described with sample type, timing measure or adjustment.

anchors.locator: Gender Differences in Substance Use Disorders › Course of Illness, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: On average women start substance use later than men (Greenfield 2010; Keyes 2010). A telescoping course, faster from first use to problems and from problems to treatment-seeking, is said to be replicated in alcohol (Diehl 2007; Randall 1999), marijuana (Khan, Okuda, et al. 2013; Lewis 2014), cocaine (Haas & Peters 2000) and prescription opioid use (Lewis 2014), but not for heroin (Lewis 2014; Stoltman 2015). One large population-based analysis (Keyes 2010) did not replicate it; a cohort explanation (Johnson 2005) is offered, but Keyes found no telescoping in any cohort.

anchors.locator: Gender Differences in Substance Use Disorders › Course of Illness, 1st paragraph (last four sentences)
anchors.extracted: Citing a previous review (Becker, McClellan & Reed 2017), the authors explain the inconsistency by study population. Telescoping was found mainly in women already in treatment, who probably have more severe disorders, while population surveys did not replicate it. So it may hold only for a subset of women vulnerable to a fast progression to severe disorders.

anchors.locator: References: Khan, Okuda, et al. (2013) and Khan, Secades-Villa, et al. (2013)
anchors.extracted: Khan, Okuda, et al. (2013), cited for marijuana telescoping, is titled as a NESARC analysis of lifetime alcohol dependence (Alcohol Clin Exp Res). The cannabis use disorder paper is Khan, Secades-Villa, et al. (2013), also NESARC (Drug Alcohol Depend 130:101–110). Both are general-population analyses.

A critical review with search terms and methods adopted from Greenfield et al. (2007). Treatment papers were limited to 2007 through April 2017; earlier seminal papers were included for etiology. In total 517 papers were reviewed for relevance. Inclusion criteria and appraisal of studies are not described.
The authors note that gender-difference findings may vary across substances, for example a telescoping course for some substances but not others, and that polydrug use in women is understudied.

claims.overstatement: The claim leaves out a qualification McHugh et al. give in the same paragraph: some evidence that women reach treatment more quickly after first use and after disorder onset (Alvanzo 2014; Blanco 2013; Lewis & Nixon 2014). That is time to treatment among people who got there, not a hazard among everyone at risk, so it does not contradict 'less likely, or slower'. But it should be reported next to the Keyes cohort-5 figure. The same paragraph says adolescent girls with alcohol use disorder were more likely than boys to receive treatment.
claims.note: All McHugh items in the claim check: 2015, women 10.4% vs men 11.1% of those needing treatment for an alcohol or drug use disorder received it (about 7.9 million women in need; CBHSQ 2016, which is NSDUH); under-treatment particularly notable among adult women with alcohol use disorder; for illicit drug use disorders, gender not associated with past-year treatment use (Compton 2007, a NESARC paper by its reference title). The paragraph also reports no gender difference in treatment entry for prescription opioid or cannabis use disorder in adults, and that men more often receive specialized treatment while women more often seek care in mental-health settings (Edlund 2012). All of it is second-hand and unappraised.

anchors.locator: Treatment of Substance Use Disorders in Women › Treatment Seeking, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: In 2015, of an estimated 7.9 million US women who needed treatment for an alcohol or drug use disorder, 10.4% received it, against 11.1% of men (CBHSQ 2016). Under-treatment is particularly notable among adult women with alcohol use disorder (Alvanzo 2014; Cohen 2007; Khan, Okuda 2013). Men more often receive specialized SUD treatment; women with SUDs more often seek care in mental-health settings (Edlund 2012).

anchors.locator: Treatment of Substance Use Disorders in Women › Treatment Seeking, 1st paragraph (opening sentences)
anchors.extracted: Some evidence is cited that women present to treatment more quickly after first use and after disorder onset (Alvanzo 2014; Blanco 2013; Lewis & Nixon 2014). Among adolescents with alcohol use disorder, girls were more likely than boys to receive treatment (Haughwout 2016).

anchors.locator: Treatment of Substance Use Disorders in Women › Treatment Seeking, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Treatment entry for illicit drug use disorders shows more gender parity. Gender was not associated with past-year treatment use (Compton 2007). There was no gender difference in treatment entry for prescription opioid use disorder (Blanco 2013; Kerridge 2015) or cannabis use disorder (Khan, Secades-Villa 2013) in adults, but adolescent boys with cannabis use disorder were more often treated than girls. In 2014 women were 46.8% of admissions for primary prescription opioid use disorder, 46.5% for tranquilizers and 58.2% for sedatives.

anchors.locator: Treatment of Substance Use Disorders in Women › Treatment Seeking, 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Barriers historically documented for women: greater perceived stigma, childcare responsibilities and lack of family support. In two population surveys, women with alcohol use disorder more often perceived stigma as a barrier; other surveys found few gender differences in barriers, possibly because they did not ask about pregnancy, childcare or family attitudes.

anchors.locator: Treatment of Substance Use Disorders in Women, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: The group's 2007 review is summarized as finding that women in general were less likely than men to seek treatment for SUDs.

claims.overstatement: The claim says that where a difference appeared it more often favoured women. This review does not support that. Most of the differences it reports go against women: smoking-cessation outcomes worse in women, nicotine replacement working better in men, poorer response to disulfiram for cocaine dependence, worse outcomes with buspirone for cannabis and cocaine, and less often completed detoxification. Varenicline relative to other aids is the one difference favouring women, and naltrexone findings are mixed. The claim's summary of women-only and gender-specific treatment cites only the null rolling-group trial from this review. It leaves out the observational findings favouring women-only programmes (43 programmes, Niv & Hser 2007; criminal-justice outcomes; Orwin 2001), the randomized support for gender-specific treatment in subgroups of women, and the closed-group pilot in which the Women's Recovery Group did better. Disulfiram: the effect is unknown in women for alcohol use disorder; for cocaine dependence women responded worse.
claims.note: The McHugh numbers in the claim all check: COMBINE (n = 1,226, 31% women; the reference title confirms it is the COMBINE gender analysis, Greenfield et al. 2010); prescription-opioid trial (n = 653, 40% women; McHugh et al. 2013, the first author's own); 24 Clinical Trials Network trials (n > 11,000; Korte 2011), no retention difference; more than 1.7 million treatment episodes (Bornstein 2015), no completion difference except detoxification; women 1.2% in disulfiram trials (as an example, via Agabio 2016); the Women's Recovery Group as effective as mixed-gender counselling in the larger trial (Greenfield 2014). The review says most studies used substance use reduction or retention as outcomes and that many trials stratify randomization by gender but do not analyse by gender.

anchors.locator: Treatment of Substance Use Disorders in Women, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: The 2007 review found that most studies showed no gender difference in treatment retention or outcome. This update covers 2007–2017: comparisons of women and men first, then gender-responsive treatment and treatment in pregnancy.

anchors.locator: Treatment of Substance Use Disorders in Women › Treatment Outcome, 2nd paragraph; References (Greenfield et al. 2010; McHugh et al. 2013)
anchors.extracted: Results are mixed, but most large randomized trials found no gender difference in outcome, including pharmacotherapy for alcohol dependence (n = 1,226, 31% women; Greenfield 2010, the COMBINE gender analysis by its reference title) and for prescription opioid dependence (n = 653, 40% women; McHugh 2013).

anchors.locator: Treatment of Substance Use Disorders in Women › Treatment Outcome, 6th paragraph
anchors.extracted: No substantive gender difference in retention: 24 NIDA Clinical Trials Network trials (n > 11,000) found no difference in trial retention (Korte 2011). Over 1.7 million US treatment episodes showed no difference in completion, except that women less often completed detoxification (Bornstein 2015).

anchors.locator: Treatment of Substance Use Disorders in Women › Treatment Outcome, 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: The exception is nicotine dependence, with worse outcomes in women (Smith 2015). Nicotine replacement works better in men (Perkins & Scott 2008). In a meta-analysis of 32 trials (n = 14,389, 51% women), varenicline against placebo was comparable by sex, but women gained more from varenicline relative to nicotine patch and bupropion (Smith 2017). With naltrexone, men cut smoking more and women gained less weight.

anchors.locator: Treatment of Substance Use Disorders in Women › Treatment Outcome, 4th paragraph
anchors.extracted: Other pharmacotherapies show no consistent gender difference. Women responded worse to disulfiram for cocaine dependence (DeVito 2014); trials of disulfiram for alcohol dependence report no such difference, perhaps because women were badly under-represented (e.g., 1.2%; Agabio 2016). Naltrexone for alcohol: mixed (men better under some dosing; no difference in COMBINE). No difference with buprenorphine or methadone. Women did worse with buspirone for cannabis and cocaine dependence, where buspirone did not beat placebo in either sex.

anchors.locator: Treatment of Substance Use Disorders in Women › Treatment Outcome, 5th and 7th paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Women and men respond similarly to behavioural therapies (cognitive-behavioural therapy, contingency management, behavioural couples therapy) and to mutual-help groups. Most studies used reduced use or abstinence and retention as outcomes; other outcomes (quality of life, mental and physical health) are unexplored.

anchors.locator: Treatment of Substance Use Disorders in Women › Gender-Specific and Gender-Responsive Treatments, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Across 43 programmes, women in women-only programmes had better drug-use outcomes than women in mixed-gender programmes despite greater severity (Niv & Hser 2007). Women-only treatment was also linked to less crime and incarceration afterwards (Hser 2011; Prendergast 2011), and to modestly better outcomes (Orwin 2001). A residential programme that switched from mixed to single-gender without other changes saw no improvement (Bride 2001, retrospective).

anchors.locator: Treatment of Substance Use Disorders in Women › Gender-Specific and Gender-Responsive Treatments, 4th paragraph
anchors.extracted: Randomized trials support gender-specific treatment for women with children, women with co-occurring disorders and women in the criminal justice system. In a closed-group pilot, the Women's Recovery Group gave greater reductions in substance use 6 months after treatment than mixed-gender group counselling (Greenfield, Trucco 2007). In the larger rolling-group trial it was as effective as mixed-gender drug counselling (Greenfield 2014), from the reviewers' own group.

The authors call the literature on treatment response limited: men and women do not substantively differ in outcomes except in smoking cessation. Many large trials stratify randomization by gender but do not analyse by gender, women are under-represented, and the efficacy of older treatments such as disulfiram for alcohol use disorder is unknown in women.

key_findings.correction: Delete 'oral': the review gives the THC doses (5 mg and 15 mg) without a route. The rest is confirmed; the doses stay study conditions only.

Minor: the text describes the 5-fold and 3-fold mortality as 'among those in SUD treatment'. 'Clinical-trial participants' comes from the reference title (Lindblad 2016, a pooled analysis of 22 Clinical Trials Network trials), which is accurate but should say so.
Minor: for illicit drug use disorders the review says gender was not associated with past-year treatment use (Compton 2007, NESARC). Add 'past-year'.

Numbers confirmed. COMBINE is named in the 4th paragraph, and the n = 1,226 trial in the 2nd paragraph is the same study by its reference (Greenfield et al. 2010, COMBINE gender analysis). See 'missed' for the other pharmacotherapy differences the finding leaves out.

Only the past-month use figures (4.7%, 13.9%, 9.3%, 21.7%) are NSDUH. The 3.6% with alcohol use disorder and 1.6% with a drug use disorder are cited to Vesga-Lopez et al. (2008), a NESARC analysis by its reference title. The 8.7% is cited to Terplan et al. (2012) and the 6.8% of facilities offering childcare to SAMHSA (2017).

reporting_issues.note: Found independently in my blind reading. Both Khan 2013 papers are NESARC general-population analyses, which sits uneasily with the review's statement that population surveys did not replicate telescoping.
Under Author Disclosures the text runs Contributors, then Conflict of Interest with only the 'all other authors' sentence.
Seedat 2009a and 2009b have identical entries (Arch Gen Psychiatry 66(7):785–795).

risk_of_bias.note: Editors' narrative-review checklist; high overall follows from unsystematic selection.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor is fair. The abstract's summary that outcomes do not substantively differ omits the pharmacotherapy differences the review itself reports, most of which go against women. That is close to the review's own 'exception' framing and does not change the rating.

missed: Treatment Outcome, 3rd and 4th paragraphs: besides smoking cessation in general, the review reports nicotine replacement working better in men (Perkins & Scott 2008), poorer response in women to disulfiram for cocaine dependence (DeVito 2014), worse outcomes in women with buspirone for cannabis and cocaine dependence (no drug–placebo difference in either sex), and mixed naltrexone findings for alcohol (men better under some dosing). Varenicline relative to other aids is the one difference favouring women. Key finding 12 should record these: they bear directly on the claim that differences more often favoured women.

Gender-Specific and Gender-Responsive Treatments, 4th paragraph: randomized trials are cited as supporting gender-specific treatment for women with children, women with co-occurring disorders and women in the criminal justice system. Key finding 14 covers only the programme comparisons and the Women's Recovery Group.
